name: Treaty at Camp Persifer F. Smith (1851), unratified California treaty D
aka: Treaty D of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 3 set apart 'forever' for the sole use and occupancy of the eleven tribes a district from the first forks of the Kern river above the Tar springs, down the Kern to Carises lake and Buena Vista lake, across to the base of the Coast Range and along it to the mouth of the Tejon pass.

Ploughs, harness, mules, oxen, axes, hoes, spades, picks and seed; a farmer, a blacksmith, a worker in wood, a superintendent and assistant school teachers, kept only so long as the President thought advisable, with a school house (Kappler, vol. 4, as excerpted by Oklahoma State University).

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty D in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States Senate, executive session; record reprinted 1905

source.title: Robert F. Heizer, The Eighteen Unratified Treaties of 1851-1852 between the California Indians and the United States Government (1972)
source.publisher: Archaeological Research Facility, University of California, Berkeley

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

source.title: Act of May 18, 1928, ch. 624, 45 Stat. 602 (Indians of California jurisdictional act)

breaches.quote: the loss to the said Indians on account of their failure to secure the lands and compensation provided for in the eighteen unratified treaties

breaches.what: The Tejon Indian Tribe states that six of its chiefs signed the 1851 treaty reserving Tejon Canyon and its surroundings, that the Senate considered the treaties in secret session, failed to ratify them and had them locked away, and that this refusal had devastating effects on Indian title, ending in a 1924 Supreme Court ruling that its title was extinguished for want of a claim under the 1851 California land claims act.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Tejon Indian Tribe, Request for Confirmation of Status to the Department of the Interior, June 30, 2006

source.title: Tejon Indian Tribe Request for Confirmation of Status (June 30, 2006), as reproduced by SCVHistory.com

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 285, 286 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

nationVoice.summary: In its 2006 request to the Interior Department to confirm its federal status, the Tribe says six Tejon chiefs, including the brothers Vincente and Chico, signed the June 10, 1851 treaty at Camp Persifer F. Smith reserving Tejon Canyon and its surroundings for the signing tribes forever, that the Senate refused to ratify it and locked it away in secret, and that this refusal ultimately devastated Indian title across California.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: Nonfederally Recognized Indian Groups.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.

In Article 3 the signing tribes gave up their claims to other lands; because the Senate rejected the treaty, the United States took the land without the reserved tract or the promised goods (1928 Act, section 2).

Audit 2026-11-08: promises corrected against treaty D as printed in Heizer (1972), the treaty text at https://digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/83366/files/arfs003-001.pdf; Heizer omits some of this treaty's articles, so the goods and staff are taken from Oklahoma State University's excerpt of Kappler vol. 4 (https://oms.library.okstate.edu/s/oklahoma-built/item/21829), and any subsistence (beef and flour) article was not checked; the earlier 'beef and flour during 1851 and 1852' line was removed because it was copied from the other treaties.

Audit 2026-11-08: the Tejon statement was reworded to what the Tribe's 2006 submission says; it does not say the Tribe was never told of the 1851 claims process, only that the 1924 ruling applied regardless of notice.
